sections.h2: What a transfer on death deed is
sections.html:
Think of it as a recorded deed that names the person who receives a Virginia property at the owner's death, with no trip through the owner's will. Under Article 5 of Title 64.2, an individual may transfer property to one or more beneficiaries effective at the transferor's death. The statute calls the owner the transferor and the person named to receive the property the designated beneficiary.

The law reaches an interest in real property in the Commonwealth. Deeds made before, on, or after July 1, 2013 are covered, provided the transferor died on or after that date. Nothing here replaces the other options: a will, a trust, or joint ownership still work.

Lawyers call the deed nontestamentary. It is a deed whose effect is delayed until death, so it follows the formalities of a deed and not the signing rules of a will.

sections.h2: What the deed must contain to be valid
sections.html:
Seven requirements appear in Va. Code 64.2-628, and a deed that misses even one can fail. Check each against your own paperwork.

  • The deed has to carry everything a normal recordable lifetime deed would.
  • Its wording must say the beneficiary receives the property when the transferor dies.
  • Recording has to happen while the transferor is alive, in the circuit court clerk's land records where the property sits.
  • Chapter 6 of Title 55.1 sets the recording rules, and the clerk indexes the deed with the transferor as grantor.
  • With no consideration involved, recordation tax does not apply.
  • Property with joint owners needs every joint owner's signature.
  • For the purposes of Va. Code 17.1-223, it is treated as a deed.

The mental capacity needed to sign or revoke is the capacity needed to make a will. Nobody has to tell the beneficiary, the beneficiary does not have to accept, and no payment is needed.

Owners can change their minds. Va. Code 64.2-625 makes the deed revocable even when the deed or another document says otherwise, and the owner stays fully in control for life.

Revoking takes a recorded document, and the law names four kinds in section 64.2-630:

  • A later transfer on death deed that expressly revokes the first, fully or partly.
  • A later transfer on death deed naming a beneficiary that conflicts with the first.
  • A stand-alone instrument of revocation stating that purpose expressly.
  • An ordinary deed to someone else, which leaves nothing owned at death.

Any revoking document must be acknowledged after the original deed was, and recorded before the owner dies in the same circuit court land records. Once a deed is recorded, destroying or marking up your copy accomplishes nothing. When several owners signed, one owner's revocation does not undo the others' share, and a deed made by joint owners is revoked only if every living joint owner revokes it. An optional revocation form appears at 64.2-636.

sections.h2: What happens at the owner's death
sections.html:
Under Va. Code 64.2-632, ownership vests in the designated beneficiary only if that person is alive when the owner dies. A beneficiary who dies first gets nothing.

Details matter when a deed names several people or a family changes over time.

  • Several beneficiaries split the property into equal undivided shares, and none has survivorship rights.
  • When one of them fails or lapses, the others absorb that share in proportion to their own.
  • A later divorce or annulment cancels a gift to the former spouse, unless the deed provides differently.
  • A surviving co-owner takes the property if the transferor was a joint owner, though still subject to the named beneficiary.

What the beneficiary gets is the property as it stood at death, burdened by every conveyance, mortgage, lien, and other interest. No covenant or warranty of title comes with it, whatever the deed says. Chapter 26 of Title 64.2 lets a beneficiary turn down some or all of the interest.

While the owner is alive, the deed changes nothing and protects the property from nobody. Section 64.2-631 spells out what it leaves alone.

  • The owner can still sell, mortgage, or otherwise deal with the property.
  • Creditors, present or future, keep every right they had, whether or not they know about the deed.
  • Public assistance eligibility stays the same for both the owner and the beneficiary.
  • The beneficiary holds no legal or equitable interest yet.
  • The property is not open to claims against the beneficiary.

Death changes things. Under section 64.2-634, property that passed by deed can be reached for creditors' claims, administration costs, funeral expenses, and family allowances, but only when the probate estate cannot cover them. If several properties passed by deed, each carries a share in proportion to its net value. Any proceeding to enforce this has to start within one year after the death.

No recordation tax is due on recording the deed, or a revocation, when nothing is paid between the parties. The exemption sits in Va. Code 58.1-811(J), and the optional statutory forms repeat the notice at the top.

That section also covers other no-payment filings that families run into.

sections.h2: Selling an inherited house held through the deed
sections.html:
With the deed in place, a beneficiary can hold title right after the death and does not have to wait for a court to open an estate for this one house. Debts stay with the house, though, and the beneficiary inherits it as is.

For a Virginia seller that works out like this:

  • Expect to hand over the recorded deed and a death record when the buyer's side wants proof you own the house.
  • Any mortgage or lien on the house is still there at closing, since the beneficiary took it subject to those.
  • Because no title warranty comes with the transfer, the title company will study the record history closely.
  • Possible estate claims under 64.2-634 may need an answer before the title company will close.

sections.h2: When this deed is the wrong tool
sections.html:
This is the wrong choice for anyone who needs a certain, permanent transfer. The owner can always revoke, and the beneficiary has no claim during the owner's life. It is also a poor fit when the owner worries the named person might die first, since a beneficiary who does not survive the owner loses the interest.

Other points to weigh with an attorney:

  • A deed recorded after the owner's death does nothing, so timing matters.
  • A deed signed by one co-owner does not bind the others, and a joint owner's deed needs every joint owner's signature to be effective.
  • Where a will leaves real estate to be sold and names no other person, the executor has the power to sell and convey under Va. Code 64.2-521, a different route from a transfer on death deed.

faqs.q: Is a transfer on death deed the same as a will?
faqs.a: No. It is nontestamentary: a recorded deed that takes effect at death. A will is a separate document that goes through probate. Signing either one takes the same capacity.

faqs.q: Does the beneficiary have to sign or accept the deed?
faqs.a: No. The deed is effective without notice to, delivery to, or acceptance by the beneficiary during the owner's life, and without consideration.

faqs.q: When must the deed be recorded?
faqs.a: Before the owner dies. It goes in the land records of the circuit court clerk's office in the county or city where the property sits, and the clerk indexes it under the owner's name as grantor.

faqs.q: Can I sell my house after recording the deed?
faqs.a: Yes. During your life the deed does not affect your right to transfer or mortgage the property. Selling by a regular deed also revokes the earlier transfer on death deed, since you no longer own the property at death.

faqs.q: What if the beneficiary dies before the owner?
faqs.a: The beneficiary's interest lapses, because it depends on surviving the owner. When several beneficiaries share the property, the lapsed share goes to the others in proportion to their interests.
